summary: Eco-Avatar Activism is a youth-led movement, launched September 10, 2023 by Palo Alto high school students, in which activists use virtual personas to promote environmental causes. Avatars are used across social media, the metaverse, gamified campaigns, virtual protests and education, with several named creators and events illustrating the trend. The article presents it as a shift in how environmental movements are conceived and carried out.
one_line: A youth-led movement uses virtual avatars on social media, the metaverse, games and virtual protests to advocate for climate and environmental causes.
key_facts: Eco-Avatar Activism was launched on September 10, 2023, by a group of high school students from Palo Alto, California.
Sixteen-year-old Zoe Chen created the avatar "GaiaX" to raise awareness about the vanishing Amazon rainforest, and it became an instant viral sensation.
Natasha Green, a 24-year-old digital artist from Toronto, creates avatars for environmental NGOs.
On October 15, 2023, the event 'Virtual Venice under Water' had thousands log in as avatars to navigate a flooded Venice simulating sea-level rise.
Jamal Carter, 18, from London uses his avatar "EcoLion" to make short animated stories about conservation efforts in Africa.
On November 2, 2023, the "Green Quest" campaign went viral, with users guiding avatars through levels by completing real-world challenges like planting a tree or going a day without plastic.
Chicago-based game developer Renee Alvarez released a smartphone app linking in-game rewards to verified real-life sustainability actions.
On December 5, 2023, the "Digital March for Earth's Rights" virtual protest mobilized more than three million avatars worldwide in an online forum designed like the United Nations.
In the protest, petitions were digitally signed and speeches were given by avatars of global activists.

Eco-Avatars collaborate with environmental scientists to share scientifically accurate information on climate change and sustainability, including in virtual classrooms where avatars serve as lecturers.
Marine biologist Katie Johnson has partnered with the avatar "CoralHeart" to teach kids about the oceans.
The movement extends beyond social media into the metaverse, where rallies and meetings occur in immersive 3D virtual environments.
